claims.text: GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev's confidence-scored decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
GeoDeploy's source code is hosted at https://github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
The Pulumi Automation API documentation is located at /docs/iac/automation-api/.
The TypeSafe Jev documentation is located at https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.
GeoDeploy picks the best AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud region for the user's users using TypeSafe's Jev paired with the Pulumi Automation API.
GeoDeploy gates every AI decision on confidence.
GeoDeploy provisions Kubernetes for the user.
GeoDeploy is open source as of the post's publication.
GeoDeploy prices every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes.
GeoDeploy asks Jev to pick the best region per geo from a closed list so that Jev cannot hallucinate a region.
GeoDeploy gates every decision on confidence, with hard rejects for data residency.
GeoDeploy provisions consistent clusters with one Pulumi stack per region.
GeoDeploy's self-driving mode scales itself, with a human in the loop when confidence is low.
TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post's publication.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives include confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
GeoDeploy answers the question of where a workload should run and what it will cost, given a set of user locations and a container image.
A GeoDeploy deployment request's target-geos part specifies where users are, what share of traffic each place sends, and any data-residency rule (EU-only, US-only, or in-country).
A GeoDeploy deployment request's image part specifies a container image and the platforms it's built for (amd64, arm64, or both).
A GeoDeploy deployment request's workload-shape part specifies replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, and storage.
A GeoDeploy deployment request's constraints part specifies which providers are allowed, how many providers will be tolerated, and a budget.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
In GeoDeploy's architecture, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing, and does all the math, but never makes judgment calls.
In GeoDeploy's architecture, Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use, but never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names.
In GeoDeploy's architecture, Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS, but never decides anything.
In GeoDeploy's pipeline, each business region (geo) is mapped to a canonical location and residency class.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost for each candidate.
Jev picks the winning region and modules for each geo in GeoDeploy's decision step.

GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules covering EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
The Pulumi Automation API runs a preview and then an update, with one stack per region, and won't run at all unless the user's cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md file with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev does not return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives.
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence score.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric the caller describes, and GeoDeploy uses 10 levels for its rubrics.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.

Jev only ever selects from closed sets, choosing among region IDs that GeoDeploy has already priced and checked, and never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates, along with the constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.
GeoDeploy's single call to Jev includes a selection question via choice() asking which region should serve a given geo.
GeoDeploy's single call to Jev includes five quality scores via score(): coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, and architecture consistency.
GeoDeploy's single call to Jev includes two hard checks via noul(): whether data residency is satisfied and whether there is enough capacity.
GeoDeploy's single call to Jev includes a fallback selection via choice() naming a backup region in case the primary fails at apply time.

The file packages/decide/src/questions.ts in the GeoDeploy repository contains a buildStageAQuestions function that imports choice, noul, and score from @typesafe-ai/sdk and constructs selection, coverage, costFit, residencyOk, and fallback questions as shown.
The options passed to Jev's choice() function are the priced candidates themselves, keyed by ID, so Jev cannot answer with a region that isn't on the list.
TypeSafe's advice is to describe situations, not degrees, when writing score() rubrics.

GeoDeploy's score() rubrics use 10 concrete-scenario levels ranging from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" up to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."

GeoDeploy sends the whole question set to Jev in one call via a TypeSafeClient's systemOne method, passing state and questions, and receives answers including selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, and coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's five scores feed a ranking system that runs on weight profiles: latency-optimized (the default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because GeoDeploy's ranking weights live in code, the ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy's WEIGHT_PROFILES constant defines four named weight profiles (latency-optimized, balanced, residency-first, failure-domain) each assigning numeric weights to cost, coverage, maturity, sprawl, and archConsistency as shown in the code sample.
In GeoDeploy's composite scoring, sprawl risk is subtracted because every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider, so that AWS always means EKS and ECR.
In GeoDeploy, Jev is left to decide ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier as open module choices.
In GeoDeploy, every Jev answer is checked against a confidence threshold matched to how risky the decision is.
In GeoDeploy, the data-residency decision has a confidence threshold of 0.95, and failing it causes a hard reject.
In GeoDeploy, the region-for-a-new-cluster decision has a confidence threshold of 0.90, and failing it flags the top three candidates for a human to choose.
In GeoDeploy, the region-when-a-stack-already-exists decision has a confidence threshold of 0.75, and failing it keeps the existing region.
In GeoDeploy, the ingress-or-autoscaling-module decision has a confidence threshold of 0.85, and failing it uses the registry default.
In GeoDeploy, the node-pool-sizing-tier decision has a confidence threshold of 0.60, and failing it uses the bin-packing result.
In GeoDeploy, the global floor confidence threshold for region pick, residency, or capacity decisions is 0.50, and failing it drops the AI path for that geo.

The file packages/decide/src/engine.ts in the GeoDeploy repository contains a residency check that applies a hard gate at the 0.95 GATE_THRESHOLDS.residencyOk threshold, throwing an AiPathAborted error if it fails, and a validation check that the selected candidate ID exists among the shortlisted candidates, also throwing AiPathAborted if not.
Each AiPathAborted error in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so even a rejected answer ends up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or returns an error, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing the residency and constraint checks.
Running `geodeploy explain` shows why each region won.

When GeoDeploy's self-driving mode is enabled via the `geodeploy monitor` command, the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with possible answers no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate check on disruption risk.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, code rather than Jev computes the actual node-count changes.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, a resize is applied automatically above 0.85 confidence.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, a resize is suggested for human approval when confidence is between 0.70 and 0.85.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, below 0.70 confidence GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric.
Using GeoDeploy requires access to Jev and a cloud provider.
Pulumi's corporate X account handle is @PulumiCorp.
Signing up for a free Pulumi account is available at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
